hints: The standard deviation of 3.8 cm comes from past experience. For the test to use it you must assume something about the standard deviation in this hot summer.

Name the population mean $\mu$. The null hypothesis says nothing has changed from 64.0; the botanist expects heights to be less than usual, so the alternative is one-tailed in the "less than" direction.

The sample mean has a normal distribution with standard deviation $\dfrac{3.8}{\sqrt{100}}$ (the $\sqrt{100}$ is there because it is a mean of 100 plants). Standardise: $z = \dfrac{63.3 - 64.0}{\ldots}$.
Work out the denominator $\dfrac{3.8}{\sqrt{100}}$ first, then divide $63.3 - 64.0$ by it and give $z$ to 3 decimal places.
For a 2.5% one-tailed test in the lower tail, the critical value is $-1.96$. Compare your $z$ with $-1.96$ — negative with negative, positive with positive.

Decide whether your $z$ is beyond $-1.96$ (in the rejection region) or not, then write the conclusion about plant heights in context, with wording like "there is (no) evidence that…" rather than a definite statement.
walkthrough:
**What kind of test this is**

We have a sample of 100 plants and want to test a claim about the **population mean height** $\mu$ (the true mean height of all plants of this variety this summer). We know a population standard deviation (3.8 cm) and the sample is large, so we use a normal test with a **z-statistic**.

**The necessary assumption (this earns the first B1)**

The 3.8 cm standard deviation was measured in past summers. To use it now we must assume it has **not changed** in the hot summer: the population standard deviation is still 3.8 cm.

Without this we would not know the spread of the sample mean and could not standardise.

**Write the hypotheses (this earns the second B1)**

The null hypothesis $\text{H}_0$ is what we assume is true until the evidence says otherwise: heights have not changed. The alternative hypothesis $\text{H}_1$ is what the botanist suspects: heights are **less** than usual. "Less" means one direction only, so it is a one-tailed test.

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 64.0 \qquad \text{H}_1: \mu < 64.0$$

Here $\mu$ is the population mean height in cm. Note that we write the hypotheses about $\mu$, not about the sample mean 63.3.

**The distribution of the sample mean under $\text{H}_0$**

If $\text{H}_0$ is true, individual heights have mean 64.0 and standard deviation 3.8. For a sample of $n = 100$ plants, the sample mean $\bar{X}$ (the average of those 100 heights) has mean 64.0 and standard deviation $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, which is smaller than 3.8 because averaging reduces the spread. Because $n$ is large, $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal.

$$\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(64.0, \left(\dfrac{3.8}{\sqrt{100}}\right)^2\right)$$

**Standardise (this earns the M1)**

To compare with the normal tables we convert to a z-value: $z = \dfrac{\text{observed} - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}$. Here the observed value is the sample mean 63.3.

$$z = \dfrac{63.3 - 64.0}{\dfrac{3.8}{\sqrt{100}}}$$

The M1 needs the $\sqrt{100}$ in the denominator. Dividing by 3.8 alone is the commonest slip: that would treat 63.3 as a single plant, not a mean of 100.

**Calculate $z$ (this earns the A1)**

Denominator first: $\sqrt{100} = 10$, so

$$\dfrac{3.8}{\sqrt{100}} = \dfrac{3.8}{10} = 0.38$$

Numerator: $63.3 - 64.0 = -0.7$.

$$z = \dfrac{-0.7}{0.38} = -1.842105\ldots = -1.842 \text{ (3 d.p.)}$$

The negative sign says the sample mean is below 64.0, which is the direction of $\text{H}_1$.

**Find what to compare it with (this starts the second M1)**

The significance level is 2.5% and the test is one-tailed in the lower tail, so we reject $\text{H}_0$ if $z$ is in the lowest 2.5% of the standard normal distribution. The boundary is the value $z_{\text{crit}}$ where $\Phi(z_{\text{crit}}) = 0.025$. By symmetry this is minus the value with $\Phi = 0.975$:

$$z_{\text{crit}} = -1.96$$

(Use the inverse-normal function on your calculator with area $0.025$, or the normal table at $0.975$ and put a minus sign.)

**Compare (this completes the M1)**

Our $z = -1.842$. The rejection region is $z < -1.96$. Compare negative with negative:

$$-1.842 > -1.96$$

so $-1.842$ is **not** far enough into the lower tail. Equivalent check with positives: $1.842 < 1.96$.

Another equivalent way is to use probabilities: $\Phi(1.842) = 0.9672$, and $0.9672 < 0.975$. All three give the same decision.

**Conclusion in context (this earns the A1 FT)**

The test statistic is not in the rejection region, so we do **not reject** $\text{H}_0$. At the 2.5% level there is not enough evidence to say the mean height has fallen. We never say "proved" or "the mean is exactly 64.0".

**Final answer**

Assumption: the standard deviation is still 3.8 cm.

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 64.0 \qquad \text{H}_1: \mu < 64.0 \qquad z = -1.842 > -1.96$$

Do not reject $\text{H}_0$: there is no evidence, at the 2.5% significance level, that the heights of this variety of plant are shorter than usual.
